sections.title: Training Plans
sections.summary: Training is an investment, not an expense — but only when aligned with the strategic plan and business needs. Training teaches the 'how' (skill); education teaches the 'why and when' (knowledge). Juran and Gryna define six planning issues. Cost-benefit analysis justifies the budget. Effective training requires reinforcement, coaching, application, and measurement. Without strategic alignment, training is the first cost cut in a downturn.

concepts.definition: Training: hands-on, applied skill acquisition — teaches HOW. Measured by demonstrating the skill and producing desired outputs. Education: formal acquisition of knowledge — teaches WHY and WHEN. Broadens thinking and knowledge base.
concepts.examTip: Memorize: Training = HOW (skill, narrow). Education = WHY/WHEN (knowledge, broad). CMQ/OE itself is mostly education.

concepts.definition: When done correctly and for the right reasons, training is not an expense — it is an investment in a workforce that differentiates the organization from competitors. Strategic asset, not overhead.
concepts.examTip: Training is the first thing cut in downturns — that's a sign it wasn't strategically aligned.

concepts.definition: (1) Quality problems and challenges faced; (2) Knowledge/skills needed to address them; (3) Existing training facilities and processes; (4) Prevailing climate (track record of past programs); (5) What needs to be done differently; (6) What's needed to gain top management support and commitment.
concepts.examTip: Juran & Gryna emphasize organizational context and management commitment, not just curriculum design.

concepts.definition: Training is most beneficial when supported by and aligned with the strategic plan. Trainees must grasp the connection between learning content and organizational strategic objectives. Management must role-model quality principles daily.
concepts.examTip: Without strategic alignment, training is seen as 'time off the line' — and is the first cost cut.

concepts.definition: Costs: trainee salaries, materials, equipment, lost production time. Benefits: employee satisfaction, improved quality, retention, reduced errors, productivity. The proposed training budget should be justified through CBA.
concepts.examTip: Always quantify benefits when proposing training — vague 'employee development' loses to hard numbers.

concepts.definition: Consistent, frequent reinforcement of practice; coaching for on-the-job recognition; timely application of skills (without reinforcement, training fades); measurement of effectiveness; addressing mainline operational needs.
concepts.examTip: Reinforcement window is critical — skills decay rapidly without immediate application.

keyFigures.title: Figure 19.1: Training vs Education Trajectory
keyFigures.description: Education shows broad, gradual knowledge growth over time. Training shows steeper measurable skill acquisition over a shorter period focused on a specific competency.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the fundamental distinction between training and education?
options: Training teaches HOW (skill); education teaches WHY and WHEN (knowledge)
practiceQuestions.explanation: Training is hands-on, applied skill acquisition — teaches HOW. Education broadens knowledge and thinking — teaches WHY and WHEN. Both are essential but serve different purposes.

practiceQuestions.q: According to Juran and Gryna, which of the following is NOT one of their six training planning issues?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The six Juran & Gryna issues focus on problems, required knowledge, existing facilities, climate, what to do differently, and management commitment. Certification fees are not on the list.

practiceQuestions.q: Why is training typically the first item cut during budget downturns?
options: It is often not aligned with strategic plans, making ROI invisible
practiceQuestions.explanation: When training isn't tied to strategic objectives with measurable outcomes, leadership sees it as discretionary overhead. Strategic alignment + ROI evidence protects training budgets.

flashcards.back: Training = HOW (skill, hands-on, narrow). Education = WHY/WHEN (knowledge, formal, broad).
(1) Quality problems; (2) Skills needed; (3) Existing facilities; (4) Climate/track record; (5) What to do differently; (6) Top management commitment.
Costs: salaries, materials, equipment, lost production. Benefits: satisfaction, quality, retention, reduced errors, productivity.

flashcards.front: Why is training often the first cost cut?
flashcards.back: Lack of strategic alignment makes ROI invisible. Tie to strategy + measure outcomes to protect the budget.

sections.title: Training Needs Analysis
sections.summary: Training cannot fix every problem. Mager and Pipe's diagnostic separates performance deficiencies from skill/knowledge deficiencies — only the latter responds to training. The J/T/F/C matrix maps gaps to Job, Training, Feedback, or Consequences solutions. Needs assessment uses surveys, performance reviews, regulatory guidelines, competency assessments, KESSA review, interviews, focus groups, and job analysis. Individual Development Plans (IDPs) anchor career growth.

concepts.definition: Training will not solve all problems. It cannot remedy poor management, lack of motivation, or root causes that aren't skill-related. Mager and Pipe: first determine if the gap is a performance deficiency or a knowledge/skill deficiency.
concepts.examTip: If a worker CAN do the job but ISN'T doing it — training is the wrong solution. Look at consequences, feedback, or system.

concepts.definition: Before committing training resources, ask: is this a performance deficiency (worker can do it but isn't) or a knowledge/skill deficiency (worker doesn't know how)? Only the latter responds to training.
concepts.examTip: Classic test question: 'Can they do it if their life depended on it?' Yes → not training. No → training.

concepts.definition: Maps the gap to a solution type: J — Job Solution (task/process redesign); T — Training Solution (knowledge/skill gap); F — Feedback (worker doesn't know how they're doing); C — Consequences (incentives or disincentives misaligned).
concepts.examTip: Memorize: J-T-F-C. Most exam questions about needs analysis hinge on choosing the right one.

concepts.definition: (1) Needs Assessment; (2) Propose Training Program (approval, funding); (3) Design and Develop Training; (4) Deliver Training; (5) Evaluate Effectiveness. Management support spans the entire process.
concepts.examTip: This is the master training process. Each phase is testable individually.

concepts.definition: Knowledge, Experience, Skills, Aptitude, Attitude — used to determine the magnitude of a training need by reviewing existing records (performance appraisals, job descriptions, completed training).
concepts.examTip: KESSA is for reviewing what employees ALREADY have, to identify gaps.

concepts.definition: (1) Review existing records (KESSA); (2) Interviews; (3) Focus groups (8–10 employees, cross-section); (4) Organizational diagnosis; (5) Job analysis (sequenced task listing, time/motion); (6) Front-end analysis (audit, root cause, competency); (7) Surveys/checklists/questionnaires; (8) Personal observation/brainstorming.
concepts.examTip: Eight techniques. Focus groups have a target size of 8–10 — common detail question.

concepts.definition: Tool that anticipates knowledge/skills/abilities needed for current and future roles. Three main elements: (1) Development goals; (2) Timelines; (3) Activities for each goal. Used for career growth, job enhancement, and succession planning.
concepts.examTip: IDP = Goals + Timelines + Activities. Three elements only — don't add fluff.

concepts.definition: Surveys, performance reviews, regulatory guidelines (safety, ISO, FDA), competency assessments. Questions to ask: Is the need mandated? Is there a specific objective? Is the need clearly defined?
concepts.examTip: Regulatory mandate is the strongest training trigger — non-discretionary.

keyFigures.title: Figure 19.2: Training Process Cycle
keyFigures.description: 5 phases: Needs Assessment → Propose Program → Design/Develop → Deliver → Evaluate Effectiveness. Management support is constant across all phases. Outcome questions: Were objectives met? What's the ROTI? Were desired outputs produced?

keyFigures.title: Table 19.2: J/T/F/C Diagnostic Matrix
keyFigures.description: Diagnostic questions map gaps to solution types: J (Job redesign), T (Training), F (Feedback), C (Consequences). Examples: 'Has TP ever done the job correctly?' 'Could TP do the job if their life depended on it?'

practiceQuestions.q: An employee knows how to perform a task correctly but consistently does not. According to Mager and Pipe, what is the appropriate solution?
options: Address consequences or feedback, not training
practiceQuestions.explanation: If the worker CAN do it but ISN'T, this is a performance deficiency, not a skill/knowledge deficiency. Training is the wrong solution. Look at feedback (F) or consequences (C) using the J/T/F/C matrix.

practiceQuestions.q: What does the acronym KESSA stand for in training needs analysis?
options: Key Elements of Successful Skills Acquisition
practiceQuestions.explanation: KESSA = Knowledge, Experience, Skills, Aptitude, Attitude. These factors are reviewed in existing employee records to determine the magnitude of a training need.

practiceQuestions.q: What are the three main elements of an Individual Development Plan (IDP)?
practiceQuestions.explanation: IDP elements: (1) Development goals, (2) Timelines to accomplish them, (3) Activities necessary for each goal. Simple structure — don't overcomplicate.

practiceQuestions.q: In the 5-phase training process cycle, which phase comes immediately AFTER needs assessment?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The 5 phases in order: (1) Needs Assessment → (2) Propose Training Program → (3) Design and Develop → (4) Deliver → (5) Evaluate. Approval and funding come before design work begins.

flashcards.back: Is this a performance deficiency (can but won't) or a skill/knowledge deficiency (can't)? Only skill gaps respond to training.
J = Job redesign. T = Training. F = Feedback. C = Consequences. Map the gap to the right one.
Knowledge, Experience, Skills, Aptitude, Attitude — factors reviewed in existing records.
(1) Needs Assessment; (2) Propose; (3) Design/Develop; (4) Deliver; (5) Evaluate. Management support throughout.
Development goals + Timelines + Activities.
8–10 employees, cross-section from work units.

sections.title: Training Materials, Development, and Delivery
sections.summary: ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation) is the foundational instructional design model. Bloom's Taxonomy categorizes learning objectives across cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains. Knowles' andragogical model (6 adult learning principles) guides design for adult learners. Delivery methods range from classroom and OJT to e-learning, gamification (4 levels), microlearning, simulation, and coaching. Job aids (8 types) substitute for or reinforce training when memory or frequency demands it.

concepts.definition: 5-phase model used by ASQ for the CMQOE program: (1) Analysis — audience, content, delivery; (2) Design — methods, measurement, evaluation criteria; (3) Development — create/purchase materials; (4) Implementation — deliver to audience; (5) Evaluation — assess results vs objectives.
concepts.examTip: ADDIE = Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate. The most-tested instructional design model on CMQ/OE.

concepts.definition: 6 levels of cognitive objectives: (1) Remember (knowledge); (2) Understand (comprehension); (3) Apply; (4) Analyze; (5) Evaluate; (6) Create (synthesis). The CMQ/OE exam uses these levels for each section.
concepts.examTip: Bloom cognitive verbs ARE the cognitive levels in the CMQ/OE BoK. Each section has a stated level.

concepts.definition: Growth in feelings/emotional areas. 5 levels: Receiving, Responding, Valuing, Organization, Characterization. Used for attitude, values, and motivation training.
concepts.examTip: Affective domain is often overlooked but critical for culture/values training.

concepts.definition: Manual/physical skills. 7 behaviors: Perception, Set, Guided Response, Mechanism, Complex Overt Response, Adaptation, Origination. Used for hands-on skill training.
concepts.examTip: Psychomotor = physical skill domain (welding, assembly, sports). 7 levels — most detailed of the three domains.

concepts.term: Knowles' Andragogy — 6 Principles of Adult Learning
concepts.definition: (1) Adults need to be self-directing; (2) Adults need to know WHY they should learn; (3) Adults are ready to learn when life requires it; (4) Adults are task/problem/life-centered (not subject-centered); (5) Adults are motivated by intrinsic AND extrinsic factors; (6) Adults bring relevant experience to the learning.
concepts.examTip: Andragogy ≠ pedagogy. Adults need WHY first, want self-direction, and learn through application — not lecture.

concepts.definition: (1) Seeing — visual demonstration; (2) Hearing — verbal explanation, paraphrasing; (3) Feeling — tactile/kinesthetic experience; (4) Doing — hands-on replication. Effective training addresses multiple styles.
concepts.examTip: See-Hear-Feel-Do. Training that uses multiple modalities outperforms single-channel delivery.

concepts.definition: New/transferred employee assigned to experienced employee who demonstrates tasks. Useful for skill training, individuals/small groups. Risk: without consistency, learners absorb wrong methods from peers. Process: tell, show, do, repeat until standards are met.
concepts.examTip: OJT must have a structured plan — informal 'shadow Joe' creates variation and bad habits.

concepts.definition: One-to-one method requiring continuous flow of instruction, comments, testing, observation, and feedback. Steps: define performance goals, identify resources, observe current performance, set expectations, plan schedule, gain commitment, give feedback, follow up.
concepts.examTip: Coaching is ongoing relationship; mentoring is broader career guidance. Don't conflate them.

concepts.definition: Level 1 — Partial Gamification (quiz/assessment in e-learning); Level 2 — Game-Based Learning (entire learning path is a game); Level 3 — Gamified Learning Path (points, badges, leaderboards); Level 4 — Gamified Portals (multi-learner interaction and competition).
concepts.examTip: Levels 1→4 = increasing immersion. Level 4 portals enable social/competitive learning at scale.

concepts.definition: Short, focused content (often video) on a specific task — and nothing more. Formats: posters, infographics, e-learning courses, games, videos, job aids, simulations, branching scenarios. Best for just-in-time learning.
concepts.examTip: Microlearning thrives because attention spans are short and tasks are specific. Pairs well with job aids.

concepts.definition: Learner builds toward mastery at their own pace. Strength: flexibility when training needs are diverse across the population.
concepts.examTip: LCI = SDL. Best when learners differ in baseline knowledge or schedule.

concepts.definition: Focuses on what students learn, how, when, and IF they learn each task. Features: learner-centered pace, job broken into manageable tasks, mastery before progression, performance-based acknowledgment, demonstrated knowledge/experience/skill.
concepts.examTip: Competency-based ≠ time-based. Move on when mastered, not when the clock runs out.

concepts.definition: (1) Task is rare and hard to remember; (2) Task is lengthy/info-intensive; (3) Cost of error is high; (4) Procedures change frequently; (5) High employee turnover with simple tasks; (6) Empowered self-sufficient roles; (7) Little time/resources for training; (8) New standards or procedures.
concepts.examTip: Job aids are training substitutes when memorization isn't practical. 8 specific use cases.

concepts.definition: Procedure manuals, laminated checklists, computer-screen prompts, nested help screens, instructions on form back, work order/traveler details, troubleshooting boards, audio guidance, decision trees.
concepts.examTip: Checklists at the workstation are the most common job aid — Atul Gawande's 'Checklist Manifesto' principle.

concepts.definition: (1) Topical outline; (2) Manuscript (full script); (3) Sentence (one sentence per topic); (4) Key word (just trigger words). Increasing flexibility but requiring more trainer expertise.
concepts.examTip: Manuscript = least flexible (read it). Key word = most flexible (presenter expertise required).

practiceQuestions.q: What does the ADDIE instructional design model stand for?
practiceQuestions.explanation: ADDIE = Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation. ASQ uses ADDIE in its CMQ/OE self-directed learning series.

practiceQuestions.q: Which level of Bloom's cognitive taxonomy represents the highest order of thinking?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bloom's cognitive levels (low to high): Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create. Create (synthesis) is the highest order.

practiceQuestions.q: According to Knowles' andragogy, what do adults need BEFORE they will engage in learning?
options: To know WHY they should learn it
practiceQuestions.explanation: Knowles' #2 principle: adults have a deep need to know WHY they should learn something. Without this, engagement and retention drop sharply.

practiceQuestions.q: Which training delivery method is BEST suited when employee turnover is high and the task is simple?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Job aids are appropriate when turnover is high and the task is simple — investing in deep training for short-tenured workers is wasteful when a checklist will suffice.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the primary risk of unstructured On-the-Job Training (OJT)?
options: Learners absorb incorrect methods from peers
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without a consistent OJT program, there is a strong possibility that people learn incorrect procedures from teammates. OJT requires a structured plan, not informal shadowing.

flashcards.back: Analysis → Design → Development → Implementation → Evaluation.
Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create.
Cognitive (mental, 6 levels), Affective (feelings, 5 levels), Psychomotor (physical, 7 levels).
(1) Self-directing; (2) Need to know WHY; (3) Ready when life requires; (4) Task/problem-centered; (5) Intrinsic + extrinsic motivation; (6) Bring experience.
Seeing, Hearing, Feeling, Doing. Use multiple channels.
L1 Partial gamification → L2 Game-based learning → L3 Gamified path (points/badges) → L4 Gamified portals (multi-learner).

flashcards.front: When to use a job aid
flashcards.back: Rare task, lengthy/info-intensive, high cost of error, frequent procedure changes, high turnover + simple task, empowerment, limited training time, new standards.
Tell them, show them, have them do it, repeat until performance standards are met.
Key word > Sentence > Topical outline > Manuscript.

sections.title: Training Effectiveness and Evaluation
sections.summary: Kirkpatrick's 4 levels (Reaction, Learning, Behavior, Results) — extended by Phillips to Level 5 (ROTI) — define training evaluation. Reaction (smile sheets) is lowest value; Results and ROTI are highest value but hardest to measure. ROTI = Net program benefits / Program costs. Rule of thumb: BCR ≥ 3:1. Failure causes include cultural resistance, lack of strategic connection, mixed participant levels, and operational logistics issues.

concepts.definition: Level 1 — Reaction: Were participants pleased? (Smile sheets, lowest value). Level 2 — Learning: Did they learn what was intended? Level 3 — Behavior: Did on-the-job behavior change? Level 4 — Results: Was there measurable organizational impact? Level 5 — ROTI: What is the dollar return on training investment? (Phillips' addition).
concepts.examTip: Memorize: Reaction → Learning → Behavior → Results → ROTI. 1 is easiest/lowest value; 5 is hardest/highest value.

concepts.definition: End-of-class survey or 'smile sheet' measuring participant satisfaction. Lowest value evaluation — being pleased ≠ having learned. Often the only level measured, which is a mistake.
concepts.examTip: Smile sheets are vanity metrics — they show comfort, not capability.

concepts.definition: Did participants learn the intended content? Measured by tests, demonstrations, certifications. The first level that measures actual capability change.
concepts.examTip: Pre-test/post-test design isolates Level 2 learning gains.

concepts.definition: Did on-the-job behavior change as a result of training? Measured by participant observation, supervisor feedback, performance appraisals. Tests transfer of learning to the workplace.
concepts.examTip: Level 3 is where training fails most often — without reinforcement, classroom learning doesn't transfer.

concepts.definition: Was there measurable organizational impact? Productivity, defect rates, customer satisfaction, retention. The most important level — but the hardest to attribute to training alone.
concepts.examTip: Attribution is the Level 4 challenge — many factors affect business results, not just training.

concepts.definition: Dollar value of training benefits divided by program costs. Phillips' addition to Kirkpatrick's original 4 levels. Highest value, most difficult to assess. Requires placing dollar values on baseline and improvement.
concepts.formula: ROTI = Net Program Benefits / Program Costs
concepts.examTip: ROTI is the executive-friendly metric. If you can't quantify ROTI, training stays a discretionary line item.

concepts.definition: Total program benefits divided by program costs. Rule of thumb: if BCR < 3:1 (less than $3 of benefit per $1 spent), the training should be considered unsuccessful.
concepts.examTip: BCR threshold of 3:1 is the de facto industry minimum. Below that, ROI is questionable.

concepts.definition: Cultural resistance from line managers; doubts about usefulness; no connection to strategic plan; no posttraining application objectives; unaddressed 'what's in it for me'; lack of line manager involvement; technique vs problem orientation; mixing participant levels; lack of in-course practice.
concepts.examTip: Most failures are organizational, not pedagogical. Line manager involvement is the #1 protective factor.

concepts.definition: Validation: measures used to assess training effectiveness (did the program do what it was supposed to do?). Verification: measures used to assess outcomes resulting from training (did learners actually achieve the desired performance?).
concepts.examTip: Validation = program effectiveness. Verification = learner outcomes. Same root concepts as ISO 9001 V&V.

concepts.term: Training, Education, and Development — Three-Way Distinction
concepts.definition: Training: skill repertoire, hands-on. Education: broadening knowledge, formal/informal. Development: longer-term acquisition of wisdom through formal and informal exposure to more experienced people — synthesizing information, accumulating insights, gaining experience and responsibility.
concepts.examTip: Training (HOW) + Education (WHY/WHEN) + Development (LONG-TERM WISDOM) = full employee growth.

keyFigures.title: Figure 19.5: Kirkpatrick/Phillips Levels of Training Evaluation
keyFigures.description: 5-level pyramid: L1 Reaction (smile sheets, lowest value) → L2 Learning (did they learn?) → L3 Behavior (did behavior change on the job?) → L4 Results (organizational impact, most important) → L5 ROTI (dollar return on investment, highest value, hardest to measure).

practiceQuestions.q: Which level of Kirkpatrick/Phillips evaluation is typically considered the LOWEST value?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Level 1 (Reaction, smile sheets) is the lowest value — participants being pleased with training does not mean they learned anything or changed behavior. It's the easiest to collect and least diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the typical rule-of-thumb minimum benefit-cost ratio (BCR) for training to be considered successful?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Industry rule of thumb: BCR ≥ 3:1 — at least $3 of benefit per $1 of training cost. Below this, training is considered unsuccessful.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the formula for Return on Training Investment (ROTI)?
practiceQuestions.explanation: ROTI = Net Program Benefits / Program Costs. Net benefits subtract baseline performance from post-training performance, then dollarized.

practiceQuestions.q: At which Kirkpatrick level do most training programs fail to deliver value, even when participants enjoyed the training?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Level 3 (Behavior) is where most training fails — without on-the-job reinforcement, coaching, and management support, classroom learning doesn't transfer to actual workplace behavior.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the difference between training evaluation 'validation' and 'verification'?
options: Validation = program effectiveness; Verification = learner outcomes achieved
Validation = before training; Verification = after training
practiceQuestions.explanation: Validation assesses whether the program did what it was supposed to do (program-level). Verification assesses whether learners actually achieved the desired performance (outcome-level). Same V&V logic as ISO 9001.

flashcards.back: L1 Reaction → L2 Learning → L3 Behavior → L4 Results → L5 ROTI. Low → high value, easy → hard to measure.
ROTI = Net Program Benefits / Program Costs.
BCR ≥ 3:1 — at least $3 benefit per $1 cost. Below = unsuccessful training.
Level 3 — Behavior. Without reinforcement and management support, classroom learning doesn't transfer to the job.
Training = HOW (skill). Education = WHY/WHEN (knowledge). Development = long-term wisdom from experience.
Validation = did the program do what it should? Verification = did learners actually achieve desired performance?
